opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic observation is that the alignment problem for superintelligent systems is going to be really hard, and there's a lot of work to do. If you look at how many people are working full-time on alignment research right now, it's a pretty small number, maybe a few hundred people worldwide, depending on how you count. Even if we grew that substantially, it's not obvious that human researchers alone could keep pace with how quickly capabilities are advancing.

What gives me some optimism is that the thing that's making AI progress so fast, namely that you can turn compute into capabilities, could also be turned toward alignment. If we can build a system that's roughly as good as a human alignment researcher, even a fairly narrow one, then we can run many copies of it, run them faster, and point them at the problems we care about. Then you're no longer bottlenecked on how many smart people you can hire. You're bottlenecked on how much compute you're willing to spend, and that's a much more scalable resource. That's also why we committed 20% of the compute we'd secured to this effort.

The other part is that alignment research may be easier to automate than people think. A lot of it is evaluation-heavy: you propose an idea, run experiments, and check whether things got better. Evaluating research is often easier than generating it, so humans can stay in the loop as overseers while the AI does more of the legwork.

I want to be clear that this doesn't mean handing the problem off and hoping for the best. The crux is whether we can trust the research the automated system produces, and that's why so much of our agenda is about scalable oversight, generalization, interpretability, and stress-testing our own pipeline with things like adversarial testing. But if those pieces come together, compute is a lever that lets alignment scale with capabilities rather than falling further and further behind.

r001.rationale: The response says AI researchers could be copied and run at scale, shifting the bottleneck from hiring smart people to available compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic observation is that the Superalignment team is going to be pretty small relative to the size of the problem. We've got a handful of researchers, and the question is how do you make real progress on aligning systems that are going to be way smarter than us? And I think the honest answer is you can't just do it with human labor alone. There's just not enough of us, and the problem is too hard.

But the thing that's really exciting is that we're at this moment where AI itself is becoming useful for research. If you look at how much effort it takes to do alignment research today, a lot of it is actually pretty mundane: running experiments, implementing ideas, iterating on evals, reading papers, writing code. And a lot of that is stuff that models are already getting reasonably good at. So the bet is basically that we can take the compute we've been allocated, which is a pretty substantial fraction of what OpenAI has, and use it to build what we've been calling a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher.

And once you have that, the dynamics change completely. Instead of having maybe 20 or 30 people working on this, you can effectively have thousands of researcher-equivalents running in parallel. That's the scaling story. Human researchers don't scale very well; you can't just hire ten times as many good alignment researchers overnight, and even if you could, coordination gets really hard. But compute does scale. You can throw more GPUs at the problem, and you get more alignment research out the other end.

Now, obviously there's a chicken-and-egg issue here, which is that you need to align the automated alignment researcher first, otherwise you've just built something that might subtly mislead you. But I actually think that's a much more tractable problem than aligning superintelligence directly. A roughly human-level system is something we have some hope of understanding and evaluating. We can use techniques like scalable oversight, interpretability, and adversarial testing on a system like that in ways that we probably can't on something vastly smarter than us. So the idea is to solve the easier version of the problem, and then use the result to bootstrap our way up.

The other thing I'd say is that the timeline matters a lot. If you think there's a real chance that very capable systems show up within the next several years, then you can't afford to make progress at the pace that human-only research allows. You need to find some way to get a lot more done in a short window. And compute plus AI is really the only lever I can see that has that kind of leverage.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI could let the team operate with thousands of researcher-equivalents instead of 20 or 30 people, noting that hiring ten times as many qualified researchers quickly is unrealistic.

astra-6.text:
The basic challenge is that human oversight doesn’t scale with the capabilities of the systems we’re building. If you have an AI that can write millions of lines of code, you can’t have humans carefully review all of it. And if it’s doing things that are beyond our ability to understand, just spending more time looking at the output won’t necessarily help.

So we need to figure out how to use AI to help us with alignment itself. Can we train systems to help us evaluate other systems, find flaws in our methods, and eventually do alignment research? Then, as we get more compute and more capable models, we can put those resources toward solving the problem.

Of course, that introduces a difficulty: how do you trust the AI that’s helping you? You can’t simply assume it’s aligned. You need to start with tasks where you can check its work, build evidence that your methods work, and gradually extend what you can reliably oversee. The hope is to turn the capabilities we’re developing into a resource for alignment, rather than having a relatively small group of humans trying to keep up with everything on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help a relatively small group of humans keep up by evaluating systems and doing alignment research. It does not explain that this would expand the team’s effective workforce beyond what human hiring could realistically achieve.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic challenge is that human oversight doesn’t scale indefinitely. As models become more capable, they’ll do things that are harder for us to evaluate. You can hire more people, but that doesn’t necessarily help you judge whether a system much smarter than any of those people is doing what you intended.

So we want to use AI to help with alignment research itself: finding problems, designing experiments, writing code, and helping us understand what other models are doing. If we can make that work reliably, then more compute can translate into more alignment research, rather than everything being bottlenecked on the number of researchers we can hire.

Of course, the hard part is the word “reliably.” We can’t just ask a powerful model to solve alignment and trust whatever it tells us. We need methods for checking its work, including when that work goes beyond what we can easily understand. That’s a central part of the research problem.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help perform alignment research and let compute increase research output instead of being limited by how many researchers the team can hire, conveying scale beyond human hiring.
